title: Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022
short_title: Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create a legal requirement for how commissioners are chosen for Australia's human rights watchdog.
The minister could only appoint someone if a public, competitive process had picked them.
No commissioner could serve longer than seven years in total, and the president would need specific expertise.
changes: Codifies a requirement for merit-based and open selection processes for Australian Human Rights Commission members.
Limits the total term for a commissioner to seven years.
Requires the President to hold suitable qualifications, knowledge or experience.
summary.affected: Members and the President of the Australian Human Rights Commission, and the Minister responsible for appointments.

divisions.question: Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 - Second Reading - Human Rights Commissioner for LGBTIQA+ people
Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 - in Committee - Human Rights Commissioner for LGBTIQA+ people

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: The bill requires that all appointments to the Australian Human Rights Commission be made through a merit-based, publicly advertised selection process, limits terms to a maximum of seven years, and establishes consistent qualification requirements for the president and commissioners—addressing concerns that led to the deferral of the commission's A‑status reaccreditation in March 2022.

speeches.speaker: Julian Leeser
speeches.brief: The coalition does not oppose the bill requiring merit-based, transparent appointments and a seven-year term limit for the Australian Human Rights Commission, arguing it is needed to retain A-status accreditation despite inconsistencies in the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions’ processes; the speaker defended the coalition’s human rights record, citing $120 million in Afghan aid, 30,000 humanitarian places, and Magnitsky-style sanctions, and thanked former commissioners including Ros Croucher, Kate Jenkins, and June Oscar.

speeches.speaker: Peta Murphy
speeches.brief: The Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection And Appointment) Bill 2022 is necessary to ensure transparent, merit-based appointments and restore public trust, as the commission itself has long advocated—citing President Rosalind Croucher’s 1 August letter and the December 2021 Free and Equal position paper. The speaker also called for a national bill or charter of human rights to provide a legislative framework for rights and responsibilities.

speeches.speaker: James Stevens
speeches.brief: The opposition supported the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022, which introduces statutory merit-based appointment processes, and thanked Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins for her workplace culture report, noting the need for cultural change in Parliament.

speeches.speaker: Zali Steggall
speeches.brief: The speech argued that the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 is needed to establish a merit-based selection process for commissioners and senior executives, addressing past politicisation that led to a deferral of A-status accreditation. It cited Grattan Institute data showing 21% of federal government board positions are political appointees, supported a new public appointments commissioner, and commended Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins as well as an amendment for a dedicated LGBTQI commissioner.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Bates
speeches.brief: The Greens moved an amendment to the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 to establish a standalone LGBTQIA+ human rights commissioner, citing higher rates of homelessness and suicide among queer and trans people as evidence of urgent need.
